newsitem.title: USA: Columbia/HCA executives charged in fraud probe.
newsitem.headline: Columbia/HCA executives charged in fraud probe.

text.p: Three Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. executives have been charged with fraud in a federal probe into an alleged billing scam at America's largest for-profit hospital chain, the Justice Department said Wednesday.
A federal grand jury in Florida indicted the executives on five counts alleging conspiracy to submit false cost reports under U.S. heath care programmes, Medicare fraud and making false statements.

More charges may be filed, U.S. Attorney Charles Wilson in Florida said in a statement. "This indictment ... represents the first phase of the government's ongoing investigation" of Columbia, he said.

In a statement, the Nashville, Tenn.-based company said it intended to cooperate fully with the government and that attorneys for the three employees would meet with the government to discuss the indictments.

"I can assure you that we take these allegations very seriously and will cooperate fully with the government," said Dr. Thomas Frist, who was named chairman of Columbia last week after the former chairman resigned under pressure.

Indicted were Jay Jarrell, chief executive of Columbia's southwest Florida division; Michael Neeb, chief financial officer of its northern Florida division, and Robert Whiteside, director of reimbursement at its headquarters.
Each defendant faces up to 25 years in prison and fines of up to $1.25 million if convicted.

Within hours of the announcement of the indictments, Jarrell appeared before a federal magistrate in Fort Myers, Fla., on conspiracy and fraud charges. He was to be released after posting a $100,000 bond, a court clerk said.
Neeb appeared before U.S. Magistrate Howard Snyder in Jacksonville, Fla. He was released on a $100,000 bond.

The clerk of the U.S. Marshal's Office in Nashville said Whiteside appeared at that office and was taken before a federal magistrate. He was later released on his own recognisance, also after posting a $100,000 bond.
Arraignment for all three was set for Aug. 19 in Fort Myers.

The executives were charged with conspiring to submit false cost reports under Medicare and the military's Civilian Health and Medical Programme on behalf of Fawcett Memorial Hospital in Port Charlotte, Fla., from 1986 until June.
The indictment was returned June 25 but was not made public until Wednesday.
Wilson said the indictment had been returned before the recent searches of various Columbia and related facilities in Florida and other states.

Earlier this month, federal agents raided 35 Columbia facilities in six states and seized files. In addition, five mid-level executives were subpoenaed in the inquiry into possible improper billing for laboratory tests, home health care and Medicare-related work.
The investigation led to the resignation under fire Friday of long-time Columbia Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Richard Scott, as well as President David Vandewater.
Frist, formerly vice chairman, said in an interview Tuesday that he intends to submit a plan to change the company and ask for time to implement it after Justice Department review.
Wilson described the case as "an important part of my office's commitment to fight against alleged fraud and abuse in our health care system."
Separately, Columbia/HCA reported earnings that contained signs the probe was hurting its results and said it was dropping plans to buy a majority stake in a health news cable television channel.

The company said net income rose to $412 million, or 62 cents a share, in the second quarter, from $364 million, or 54 cents a share, a year earlier -- as Wall Street expected. Sales grew to $5.2 billion from $4.9 billion.

But analysts said key indicators were less encouraging. Columbia reported a 6 percent rise in revenues at hospitals open at least a year -- above the industry average of 5 percent but below the company's usual range of 7 to 11 percent.

"They definitely showed signs of slowing momentum. And this is the first quarter where there's any impact at all (from the federal investigation). So you know it's going to get worse," said Margo Vignola, health care industry analyst at Merrill Lynch.

Columbia also said it had decided not to proceed with an agreement announced May 13 to buy a majority interest in America's Health Network, the 24-hour health news cable channel, from A.H. Belo Corp., based in Dallas. Terms were not disclosed.
